topic: Eigenvectors, Eigenvalues, and Eigenbasis: The Geometry of Linear Transformations

sections.title: The Intuition: Stretching vs. Rotating
sections.content: Introduce linear transformations as 'stretching' space. Most vectors change direction when transformed. However, some special vectors stay on their original 'span' (line). These are the 'eigen-directions'.
sections.example: Visualize a grid of rubber being pulled diagonally. Most arrows point to new directions, but the arrows pointing along the pull axis remain stuck on their original lines.

sections.title: Defining the Eigen-Pair
sections.content: Define the equation Av = λv. 'A' is the transformation, 'v' is the eigenvector (the direction that doesn't change), and 'λ' (lambda) is the eigenvalue (the scalar factor of stretch or shrink).
sections.example: Imagine a 2D robot arm. If the arm moves, an eigenvector is the 'axis' of the arm that only changes length, not orientation. λ > 1 means it stretches; λ < 1 means it shrinks; λ = -1 means it flips.

sections.title: Constructing the Eigenbasis
sections.content: If we have enough linearly independent eigenvectors, they form an 'eigenbasis'. In this coordinate system, the matrix A becomes a simple diagonal matrix, making complex transformations computationally trivial.
sections.example: Think of a chaotic cloud of bird migration. If we use the 'eigenbasis' (the primary paths of travel), the complex matrix describing the flock becomes a simple set of independent growth rates.

sections.title: Visual Summary & Practical Application
sections.content: Connect the math to the 'Eigenface' concept. By finding the eigenvectors of a face database, we can represent any face as a combination of 'eigen-features' rather than raw pixels.
sections.example: A security system identifying a face by assigning weights to 'eigen-noses' and 'eigen-eyes' instead of analyzing every single pixel.
